Scams targeting seniors—criminals specifically targeting the elderly population because this age group has lower technological literacy—have become an increasingly serious problem in the United States.

According to Incogni's analysis of FBI data, 72% of senior fraud cases in 2024 were successful due to victims' personal information being exposed online, with losses reaching $4.2 billion.

How these scams work

Family chat groups are a treasure trove for scammers. Everyday sharing—from doctor visits to travel plans—provides personalized information that makes it easier for them to convincingly impersonate a family member in distress.

Given that iMessage, WhatsApp, and most other messaging apps use end-to-end encryption, you might think this information is completely secure, but that's not the case. One of the most dangerous tools commonly used by scammers is the so-called "SIM swap."

They will use any personal information found from public sources to try to convince mobile carriers that they are the target person. They claim the phone has been lost or damaged and ask the carrier to transfer the number to a new SIM card they have already purchased.

Once the carrier is deceived, all text messages sent to the victim will be received by the scammer instead. This includes SMS two-factor authentication codes used to reset passwords, log into bank accounts, and more. It is precisely this capability that allows scammers to gain access to family chat groups.

They combine personal information already obtained from the internet with further details extracted from chats, which is enough to convincingly persuade victims that they are indeed a family member in urgent need of help. This even includes voice messages, providing recordings needed to create deepfake voices that sound exactly like that family member.

How to protect your family

You can take three main steps to protect your family from these types of attacks.

First, minimize the personal information that scammers can find online. Scammers will use people-search sites to obtain information such as family members' names and phone numbers, as well as details like hobbies and travel records. There are hundreds of such people-search sites, and removing your data from all of them is an extremely daunting task. Fortunately, Incogni can do it for you.

Second, make sure two-factor authentication (2FA) is enabled on all messaging apps and social media. Ultimately, whenever you have the option to use two-factor authentication, you should enable it. If the system lets you choose between receiving codes via SMS or an authenticator app, always choose the app. This is the best safeguard against SIM swap attacks.

Third, you must contact that family member through another method to confirm they are really who they say they are. For example, if you receive a text message, reply by email instead; if you receive an email, call the person instead. The more communication channels scammers need to break through, the lower their chances of success.

Finally, agree on a "secret password" known only to family members, to be used to verify identity during emergency calls. If you receive a call from someone claiming to be a family member in urgent need of help, even if you think you recognize their voice and they seem to know a lot of personal details, you must always ask them for the password. This is the last line of defense when scammers have already obtained your family member's phone number, email account, and other information.
